strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: UI-to-code generation is practically useful, visually demanding, and naturally benefits from rendered feedback. The interactive formulation combining initial generation, polishing, and editing is well motivated.

UI2CodeN is a substantial systems/model contribution. The manuscript describes a coherent three-stage recipe: large-scale UI-code continual pretraining, SFT for UI-to-code/polishing/editing, and RL with visual rewards.

The reported empirical gains are large. UI2CodeN-9B-RL substantially improves over open-source VLMs on Design2Code, Flame-React-Eval, Web2Code, the proposed UI2Code-Real benchmark, and UI polishing benchmarks, and is competitive with strong closed-source models in several settings.

The reward-design ablations are useful. The paper compares CLIP rewards, VLM rewards, comparator scoring, and round-robin comparison, and the results support the claim that reward quality matters for RL in this domain.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful qualitative examples and appendices that specify the VLM-judge prompts and reward algorithms.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence relies heavily on VLM-as-judge metrics, but the paper does not provide sufficient validation against human judgments. This is especially concerning because the method also trains with VLM-based rewards, so the reported improvements may partly reflect optimization toward judge preferences rather than true UI fidelity or developer usefulness.

Reproducibility is weak for a paper making open-source and training-recipe claims. The abstract says code and models are available but the URL is blank, and many key details are underspecified: crawl sources and filtering, exact SFT generation prompts/procedures, verifier fine-tuning data, rendering environment, compute budget, decoding parameters, and benchmark release details.

The new benchmarks are small and not sufficiently characterized: UI2Code-Real has 115 webpages and UIPolish subsets have 100 examples each. There is little discussion of sampling, deduplication, contamination with training/crawled webpages, task difficulty distribution, or whether closed/open models were evaluated under identical prompting and inference budgets.

The claims are sometimes stronger than the evidence. The paper claims a new paradigm and state-of-the-art performance comparable to GPT-5/Claude/Gemini, but test-time scaling is only demonstrated on self-constructed benchmarks, with modest absolute gains, and no analysis of inference cost, failure modes, or when iterative polishing degrades outputs.

The RL setup raises methodological concerns. Removing KL and entropy regularization is asserted to improve stability, but no direct ablation is shown. The round-robin verifier requires O(N^2) VLM calls, yet the paper does not quantify training cost or scalability.

There is no meaningful limitations or ethics discussion. This is a notable omission given the use of large-scale crawled webpages, possible copyrighted UI/code data, privacy risks in web screenshots, generated-code security concerns, and downstream impacts on frontend development labor.

Presentation has several polish issues that reduce confidence: the missing repository link, occasional grammar errors, inconsistent naming such as UI2CodeN/UI2Code-Real, and some evaluation details deferred or left vague.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically useful problem: generating and iteratively refining executable UI code from screenshots, where visual feedback is genuinely relevant to real front-end workflows.
The interactive formulation combining UI-to-code, UI polishing, and UI editing is sensible, and the test-time polishing idea is a natural way to exploit rendered feedback.

The manuscript reports broad comparisons across public benchmarks and new real/synthetic polishing benchmarks, and includes ablations on reward design and real-world RL data that partially support some design choices.
The system-level effort appears substantial: large-scale continued pretraining, SFT, RL, verifier design, and benchmark construction are all brought together in one UI-coding pipeline.
weaknesses: The main empirical evidence is not sufficiently trustworthy. Most key results rely on VLM-as-judge evaluation, with UI-to-code scored by o4-mini and polishing by Gemini-2.5-Pro, but the paper provides no human validation, inter-rater agreement, judge sensitivity analysis, or calibration study showing that these scores reliably track actual UI fidelity.

The training reward and evaluation protocol are closely entangled with VLM judging. Since RL optimizes VLM-based rewards and the headline metrics are also VLM-judged threshold accuracies, the gains may partly reflect reward/evaluator alignment rather than true visual or functional improvement.

The new benchmarks are small and underspecified: UI2Code-Real has only 115 examples and UIPolish has 100 real plus 100 synthetic examples. There is little detail on collection, filtering, release, prompt protocol, rendering environment, or possible overlap with the authors' large web crawl and RL data.

Reproducibility is weak despite the claim of a full training recipe. The 10M crawl, synthetic SFT generation process, verifier fine-tuning data, model prompts for baselines, rendering stack, compute budget, sampling settings, and train/test decontamination procedures are not described in enough detail for others to reproduce or audit the results.

Several claims are overstrong. Statements such as surpassing leading closed-source VLMs and providing the first full training recipe are not convincingly established, especially given dependence on small self-curated benchmarks and automatic judges.

The ablations are too limited for the scale of the claims. They do not isolate the contributions of pretraining, SFT data types, UI editing data, RL data mixture, verifier fine-tuning, or iterative polishing cost; the polishing reward ablation shows only modest gains over SFT on small benchmarks.

The paper gives almost no meaningful limitations or ethics discussion. This is problematic because the work involves large-scale crawling of webpages/screenshots/HTML, possible licensing and privacy issues, use of proprietary models to generate training data and evaluations, and potential downstream misuse for cloning website designs.

Presentation is generally readable, but important methodological details are replaced by high-level descriptions, and some wording is promotional relative to the strength of the evidence. The abstract also contains an incomplete availability statement.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and timely problem: generating high-fidelity UI code from screenshots and improving it through rendered visual feedback, which is closer to real front-end development than one-shot screenshot-to-code generation.

The proposed interactive UI-to-code formulation is compelling. Separating UI-to-code, UI polishing, and UI editing gives the work a broader and more useful task framing than standard single-turn generation, and the reported test-time scaling results show clear gains from repeated polishing.

The empirical results are strong relative to open-source VLM baselines. UI2CodeN-9B-RL substantially improves over GLM-4.1V-9B and other open models across Design2Code, Flame-React-Eval, Web2Code, UI2Code-Real, and the polishing benchmarks, and in several cases approaches or exceeds closed-source systems.

The multi-stage training recipe is well motivated: large-scale real webpage pretraining, curated SFT for UI-to-code/polishing/editing, and RL using rendered visual feedback address real limitations of available UI-code data.

The ablations are useful and support important design choices, especially the comparison of CLIP versus VLM rewards, the round-robin comparator for polishing, and the role of real webpages in the RL stage.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies heavily on VLM-as-a-judge metrics, including o4-mini for UI-to-code and Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing. This is reasonable for the domain but not fully convincing without stronger human validation, inter-rater checks, or calibration analysis, especially because the claimed improvements are largely measured by proprietary judge models.

Reproducibility is weaker than the paper suggests. The abstract says code and models are available, but the manuscript text contains no visible URL; many crucial details of the 10M-page crawl, filtering, SFT data generation, verifier fine-tuning data, benchmark release, rendering environment, and prompts/hyperparameters for compared models are either missing or only lightly specified.

The self-constructed UI2Code-Real and UIPolish benchmarks are small and insufficiently documented. The paper does not clearly describe sampling, deduplication, train/test contamination checks, license status, or whether these benchmarks overlap with crawled pretraining/RL webpages.

The comparison to agentic UI-to-code systems is incomplete. The related work discusses ScreenCoder, DCGen, and similar workflows, but the main table compares mostly base VLMs rather than strong interactive or agent-based systems that may be more directly competitive with the proposed paradigm.

The RL reward and evaluation setup create possible circularity concerns: VLM-based reward optimization is evaluated with other VLM judges, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze whether the model learns judge-specific preferences rather than genuinely better visual/code fidelity.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics discussion. This is important given large-scale web crawling, possible copyright/licensing issues, privacy leakage from real webpages, accessibility concerns in generated UI, and misuse risks such as automated imitation of existing websites or phishing pages.

Some presentation details reduce confidence: several claims are overstated, such as 'first' and 'full training recipe' claims; there are minor grammar issues; and the UI editing capability is mostly shown qualitatively rather than evaluated quantitatively.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: screenshot-to-front-end code generation, where executable visual feedback is naturally useful and practically meaningful.
The interactive formulation unifies drafting, polishing, and editing in a clean way, and the iterative refinement results are compelling evidence that test-time feedback can improve UI fidelity.

The proposed RVPO training objective is sensible for non-differentiable rendered outputs: using relative/tournament preferences is better matched to visual comparison than poorly calibrated absolute scores.

The empirical section is broad, covering public benchmarks, new real-world and polishing benchmarks, ablations over reward design and training stages, human evaluation, evaluator stability, and comparisons to agent-based systems.
The paper includes useful ethics and data-governance discussion, including crawler constraints, PII filtering, and some decontamination procedures.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims rely heavily on VLM-as-judge accuracy thresholds and pairwise judgments, including closed or evolving evaluators such as o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and GPT-5. The human validation is helpful but relatively small and not enough to fully support strong SOTA claims over closed-source systems.

Reproducibility is limited. The model is described as open-source, but the manuscript does not provide concrete release details, checkpoints, code, prompts/scripts for rendering, benchmark samples, or verifier checkpoints. Several datasets are crawled or not released, and some evaluation depends on closed APIs.

The novelty of RVPO is somewhat incremental: it is essentially tournament-style relative rewards combined with GRPO/RLAIF-style optimization. The paper would benefit from clearer positioning against preference optimization and RL-from-AI-feedback methods beyond application-specific framing.

There are internal inconsistencies and unclear details. The method is alternately called RVPO and VRPO; the appendix describes absolute verifier rewards for drafting despite the main contribution emphasizing relative optimization; and the relationship between the reward verifier, evaluation judge, teacher labels, and held-out evaluators is not always cleanly separated.

Potential data leakage and contamination remain a concern. The paper trains on large crawled web data and evaluates on web-derived benchmarks; hash-based image deduplication and benchmark disjointness statements are not sufficient to rule out overlap through URLs, templates, assets, or near-duplicate pages.

The new benchmarks, UI2Code-Real and UIPolish-bench, are small and self-curated, and their construction/annotation details are not sufficient for independent assessment. This weakens claims about real-world generalization.

The human studies need more methodological detail: annotator expertise, blinding, inter-annotator agreement, UI display protocol, randomization, and statistical significance are either absent or under-specified.

The paper makes strong claims about structurally reasonable code, but evaluation is still mostly screenshot-level. Absolute-positioning ratio alone is too narrow to establish maintainability, semantic correctness, accessibility, responsiveness, or functional front-end quality.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: improving UI-to-code generation using rendered execution feedback rather than treating it as a one-shot screenshot-to-code task.

The proposed closed-loop framing for drafting, polishing, and editing is coherent, and the paper reports a broad set of experiments across public benchmarks, newly curated real-world/polishing benchmarks, human preference studies, ablations, and efficiency comparisons.

The empirical results suggest that the trained 9B model can be competitive with much larger open and closed models on several UI generation and polishing tasks, especially when evaluated by the authors' VLM-based protocols.
The appendices include useful implementation details for training stages, verifier prompts, RL settings, and some analyses of evaluator stability, reward hacking, and polishing oscillations.
weaknesses: The central claims depend heavily on VLM-based judges whose validity is not established strongly enough. The main metric is a thresholded o4-mini or Gemini score, and many headline gains over closed-source systems are therefore evaluator-dependent. Human validation is small, uses limited annotators, and reports aggregate agreement without enough detail on instructions, blinding, inter-annotator reliability, confidence intervals, or statistical significance.

There is substantial circularity and risk of evaluator overfitting: the reward/comparator is fine-tuned from Gemini-2.5-Pro preferences, polishing evaluation also uses Gemini-2.5-Pro, and the model is optimized directly against VLM visual judgments. The paper does not convincingly show that improvements transfer to independent human judgments at sufficient scale.

The methodological novelty is modest. RVPO is essentially GRPO with tournament-style pairwise VLM rewards, and the paper does not clearly distinguish this from existing preference/RLAIF-style optimization beyond the UI setting. Some terminology is inconsistent, e.g. RVPO versus VRPO, and the paper sometimes claims relative optimization while Appendix A describes absolute scalar reward for UI drafting.

Reproducibility is weak. The work relies on a large 10M-pair crawled corpus, 80K SFT samples, 42K RL samples, fine-tuned reward verifiers, newly curated benchmarks, and an early GLM-4.1V checkpoint, but does not provide enough concrete data construction, filtering, release, checkpoint, rendering-environment, or training infrastructure details for independent replication.

The new benchmarks are underspecified. UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench, and UIEdit-Bench are described only at a high level, with limited information about selection criteria, licenses, deduplication, difficulty distribution, and whether they will be released. This makes the strongest reported results hard to verify.

The evidence for state-of-the-art performance is mixed. On traditional structural metrics, UI2CodeN-RL is often comparable to but not clearly better than GPT-5/Gemini/Claude; the strongest superiority claims come from the authors' VLM judge and private benchmarks. The paper also lacks rigorous statistical testing for small benchmarks such as Flame-React-Eval and the 80-sample HARD subset.

Some results are internally awkward or underexplained. The polishing analysis reports average polishing accuracy decreasing from round 1 to round 3 before recovering, despite the main narrative of consistent iterative improvement. The explanation that regressions are merely stylistic is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The limitations and ethics discussion is inadequate for a large-scale web-crawled UI-code model. It asserts robots.txt compliance, PII removal, copyright mitigation, and research-only release, but gives few auditable details. Potential leakage from Common Crawl and public UI benchmarks is addressed only with image hashing, which is insufficient for webpage/code overlap.

Presentation is polished but often overclaims. The paper repeatedly states that the model outperforms substantially larger closed-source systems, but the evidence is conditional on private data, VLM judges, and limited human evaluation. A more cautious framing would be needed before others could reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Timely and significant problem formulation: recasting UI-to-code as closed-loop visual optimization matches real frontend workflows better than one-shot generation, and the paper clearly unifies drafting, polishing, and editing under this view.

Strong empirical results across many baselines and tasks. The 9B UI2CodeN-RL model is competitive with or better than much larger open and closed models on Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code, UI2Code-Real, UI polishing, and UI editing evaluations.

The RVPO idea is technically sensible: relative/tournament-based visual preferences are a good fit for noisy, poorly calibrated visual judges, and the ablations show consistent gains over SFT and absolute-reward alternatives.

The paper makes a serious effort to validate automated evaluation, including human pairwise studies, sample-level score calibration, repeated-run variance analysis, held-out evaluator checks, and comparisons with agent-based systems.
Presentation is generally clear and complete, with useful appendices covering verifier prompts, training details, benchmark descriptions, ethics, reward hacking analysis, and additional ablations.
weaknesses: The central evidence still depends heavily on VLM-as-judge evaluation. Although the human validation is helpful, the main metrics are thresholded automated scores, and the threshold of 80 is somewhat arbitrary; small differences among top models may not always translate into robust user-perceived superiority.

Originality is meaningful but not exceptional: RVPO is largely a domain-specific application of relative preference optimization/GRPO with visual judges, and the conceptual shift to iterative rendering feedback is natural for UI generation.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The model is described as open-source, but the large crawled training corpus, newly introduced benchmarks, verifier fine-tuning data, and use of closed/commercial teacher or evaluator models may be hard for independent groups to exactly reproduce.

Several claims about code quality and practical frontend usefulness are under-evaluated. The paper mainly measures screenshot fidelity; accessibility, responsiveness, semantic HTML quality, maintainability, interactivity, and cross-browser behavior receive little direct evaluation.

The benchmark and human evaluation sample sizes for some new settings are modest, especially UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-Real/Synthetic, Design2Code-HARD human comparisons, and UIEdit-Bench. More statistical testing would strengthen confidence in close comparisons.

There are some presentation and consistency issues, including RVPO/VRPO naming inconsistency and occasional typos. These are minor, but they slightly reduce polish for a paper making strong empirical claims.

The ethics and data governance discussion is responsible in tone, but remains high-level. Claims about robots.txt compliance, PII filtering, copyright filtering, and decontamination would benefit from more auditable procedures or release artifacts.
